title: Form Validation Patterns Without a Library

subChunks.title: Form Validation Patterns Without a Library
subChunks.hookHtml: Before reaching for a form library, understand what validation actually is: a function that takes form values and returns error messages. That's it. React state is already perfectly capable of holding error messages, and controlled inputs give you the values to validate at any moment. Knowing how to build validation from first principles makes you a better user of form libraries later — because you understand what they're doing under the hood.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The validation state pattern

Validation needs two things: form values (already in state as controlled inputs) and error messages (a separate state object keyed by field name):

const [values, setValues] = useState({ email: '', password: '' });
const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});

// On submit, validate and either submit or show errors:
function handleSubmit(e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const newErrors = validate(values);
  setErrors(newErrors);
  if (Object.keys(newErrors).length === 0) {
    // No errors — proceed
    submitForm(values);
  }
}

The validate function

A pure function that takes values and returns an errors object. Empty object means valid:

function validate(values) {
  const errors = {};

  if (!values.email) {
    errors.email = 'Email is required';
  } else if (!values.email.includes('@')) {
    errors.email = 'Enter a valid email address';
  }

  if (!values.password) {
    errors.password = 'Password is required';
  } else if (values.password.length < 8) {
    errors.password = 'Password must be at least 8 characters';
  }

  return errors;
}

Displaying errors

function LoginForm() {
  const [values, setValues] = useState({ email: '', password: '' });
  const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});

  function handleChange(e) {
    const { name, value } = e.target;
    setValues(prev => ({ ...prev, [name]: value }));
    // Clear the error for this field as the user types:
    if (errors[name]) setErrors(prev => ({ ...prev, [name]: '' }));
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <div>
        <input name="email" value={values.email} onChange={handleChange} />
        {errors.email && <p className="error">{errors.email}</p>}
      </div>
      <div>
        <input name="password" type="password" value={values.password} onChange={handleChange} />
        {errors.password && <p className="error">{errors.password}</p>}
      </div>
      <button type="submit">Login</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Touched state — don't show errors before the user has seen the field

Show errors only for fields the user has actually interacted with:

const [touched, setTouched] = useState({});

function handleBlur(e) {
  setTouched(prev => ({ ...prev, [e.target.name]: true }));
}

// Only render the error if the field has been touched:
{touched.email && errors.email && <p className="error">{errors.email}</p>}

Vex: "Never show an error before the user has had a chance to fill in the field. That's the form yelling at someone who just arrived. Wait until they blur out of the field — that's when they've finished their attempt and are ready to hear feedback."

Derived: isValid and isSubmittable

// Derived — recomputed every render:
const isValid = Object.keys(validate(values)).length === 0;

// Disable the submit button until the form is valid:
<button type="submit" disabled={!isValid}>Submit</button>

Async validation (username availability etc.)

async function handleUsernameBlur() {
  setTouched(prev => ({ ...prev, username: true }));
  const taken = await checkUsernameAvailability(values.username);
  if (taken) {
    setErrors(prev => ({ ...prev, username: 'Username is taken' }));
  }
}

storyBeats.text: Vex lays out a scroll on the bench — a contract. She points to the signature line. 'You do not scold someone the moment they pick up the quill,' she says. 'You wait until they have tried to sign. Then, if the signature is wrong, you tell them why.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Validation is a pure function. Values in, errors out. The form library you'll use in Senior tier is just this pattern with more features — touched state, async validation, schema integration. If you understand how to write it by hand, no library will ever be a black box.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a RegistrationForm with validation:

  • Fields: username (required, min 3 chars), email (required, must contain @), password (required, min 8 chars)
  • Show errors only after submit is attempted — use a submitted boolean state
  • Display each error in a <p data-testid="{field}-error"> element below its input
  • Disable the submit button when any error is showing (i.e. after a failed submit)
  • On successful validation, show <p data-testid="success">Registered!</p>

guidedPracticeTests.label: Submit with empty form shows username error
Submit with empty form shows email error

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <CheckoutForm> from scratch. Fields: cardName (required), cardNumber (required, exactly 16 digits), expiry (required, format MM/YY), cvv (required, 3 digits). Use touched state so errors only appear after each field is blurred. Derive isValid from the validate function and disable the submit button while the form is invalid. On success, show an order confirmation message.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the touched state pattern to a developer who is frustrated that their form shows all errors immediately on page load. Why do we need touched state, how does it interact with the validate function, and how does it improve the user experience? Walk through the lifecycle of a single field from first focus to showing a valid error message.

questions.prompt: A `validate` function for a form receives the current values object. What should it return?
options: An object where keys are field names and values are error message strings — empty object means the form is valid
A boolean: true if valid, false if not
An array of error message strings
A Promise that resolves to the validated data
questions.answer: An object where keys are field names and values are error message strings — empty object means the form is valid
questions.explanation:
The idiomatic React validation pattern returns an errors object keyed by field name. This makes it easy to render field-specific error messages: `errors.email &&

{errors.email}

`. An empty object (`{}`) means no errors — the form is valid. A boolean loses field-level detail. An array requires a mapping step to connect errors to fields.

questions.prompt: What is 'touched' state in form validation, and when should errors be shown?
options: A record of which fields the user has interacted with; errors should only show for touched fields
A boolean that tracks whether the form has been submitted at least once
A special React state type for sensitive form data that gets cleared on re-render
CSS state applied to a field when it receives focus
questions.answer: A record of which fields the user has interacted with; errors should only show for touched fields
questions.explanation: Touched state is typically an object like `{ email: true, password: false }` — set to true when a field fires onBlur. Errors are only rendered when `touched[fieldName]` is true. This prevents error messages appearing on fields the user hasn't visited yet, which is jarring. The field is validated on every keystroke, but the error is only displayed after the user has engaged with it.

questions.prompt: When should you reach for a form library (like React Hook Form or Formik) vs. building validation by hand?
options: For forms with complex validation (async, cross-field rules, schema-based) or many fields; for simple 2-3 field forms, hand-rolled validation is cleaner
Always use a library — hand-rolled validation is never acceptable in production code
Only use a library when the designer provides a validation spec — otherwise hand-roll
Libraries are for server-side validation; hand-rolled code is for client-side validation
questions.answer: For forms with complex validation (async, cross-field rules, schema-based) or many fields; for simple 2-3 field forms, hand-rolled validation is cleaner
questions.explanation: A library pays for itself when you need async validation, Yup/Zod schema integration, cross-field dependencies, dirty/pristine tracking, or performance optimisation for large forms. For a login form or a 3-field contact form, hand-rolled validation is simpler and adds zero dependencies. Understanding both prepares you to choose deliberately rather than reflexively reaching for a library.
